newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan PM calls talks with India breakthrough.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan PM calls talks with India breakthrough.

text.p: Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Monday described an agreement with arch-foe India on an agenda for future talks as a major breakthrough because it included the dispute over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.

The state radio quoted him as saying it was the first time India had recognised Kashmir as disputed, as he referred to a joint statement issued in the morning after four-day peace talks between top foreign ministry officials of the two countries.
"It is a major breakthrough in Indo-Pakistan relations," Sharif told reporters at parliament.
He said his government would sincerely continue the process of dialogue with India for solving disputes and hoped it would be productive.

But a Pakistan-based leader of a militant group fighting Indian rule in two-thirds of Jammu and Kashmir region, Amanullah Khan, denounced the Indo-Pakistan statement for not referring to what he called Kashmir people's self-determination right and not recognising them as a party to the dispute.
Pakistan controls the remaining third of Kashmir, over which the two countries have fought two of their three wars since their independence from Britain in 1947.

Khan, whose Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front seeks to reunite the region into an independent state, said in a statement that for Kashmiris, Monday's joint statement was "far worse" than a 1972 Indo-Pakistan peace accord in which the two sides pledged to solve the issue through bilateral talks.
"In short, the joint statement was a complete disappointment to patriotic Kashmiris," he said.

Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, speaking in parliament, called the Islamabad talks a success that had opened up an opportunity for promoting friendly and a harmonious relationship between the two countries.
"It is a very progressive step and our satisfaction is that for the first time the issue of Jammu and Kashmir has been put on the agenda for working groups along with other issues," he said.
"Now, step by step, we will go ahead to solve the much important and the long-standing Jammu and Kashmir problem."

The joint statement issued after the talks between the Indian and Pakistani foreign ministry secretaries, or top career diplomats, said the two sides had agreed to set up working groups to tackle all outstanding issues dividing them.
India and Pakistan, both seen as threshold nuclear powers, agreed to halt hostile propaganda and avoid provocative actions.
Topping the agenda was "peace and security, including CBMs (confidence-building measures)", with Jammu and Kashmir second.
India and Pakistan agreed to discuss their confrontation on the Siachen glacier, terrorism and drug trafficking, economic and commercial cooperation, and other issues.
